titleText.es: Oye, ¿por qué eres TÚ el presidente del Club de la Tautolog... vale, me lo imagino.
titleText.en: Hey, why do YOU get to be the president of Tautology Clu-- wait, I can guess.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish text is the exact title attribute in the Spanish archive; the English text is the exact official xkcd title attribute.

regions.labelEs: UN MOMENTO. ¿DEBO UNIRME A ESTA SOCIEDAD DE HONOR PARA DEMOSTRARLE A MIS COLEGAS QUE SOY HONORABLE, Y SOY HONORABLE PORQUE PERTENEZCO A UNA SOCIEDAD DE HONOR?

applications.explanationEn: Un momento is used as a brief interruption asking the listener to pause.
Debo changes for the speaker, while unirme keeps the action verb in its unchanged -ir form.
The pronominal verb unirse appears in its unchanged form, with me replacing se and attaching to the end for the speaker.

applications.exampleEs: UNIRME A ESTA SOCIEDAD DE HONOR
applications.explanationEn: Unirme supplies the speaker's form of unirse, and a introduces the complete group being joined.
The three-word institutional expression names an honor society.
Para introduces the purpose, and demostrarle keeps demostrar in its unchanged dictionary form.
Le is attached to the end of the unchanged verb demostrar to mark the receiver.

Le inside demostrarle marks the receiver, while a mis colegas names that receiver explicitly. Because colegas is plural, careful standard Spanish normally uses demostrarles; the raster preserves singular le.

applications.exampleEs: PERTENEZCO A UNA SOCIEDAD DE HONOR
applications.explanationEn: Pertenezco changes for the speaker, and a introduces the complete group to which the speaker belongs.
The same three-word institutional expression appears again as the group whose membership is being discussed.
The ordinary statement order begins with debo and becomes a yes-or-no question through question marks and intonation, without an extra Spanish equivalent of English ‘do.’
The adjective básica takes its feminine singular form before -mente is added.

regions.labelEs: ME PARECE QUE PODRÍA AHORRARME TIEMPO UNIÉNDOME DIRECTAMENTE AL CLUB DE LA TAUTOLOGÍA.

applications.explanationEn: Parece and que form the conventional introduction to the speaker's impression.
Podría changes for the speaker's possible option, while ahorrarme keeps ahorrar in its unchanged -ar form.
Ahorrar remains in its unchanged form, and me attaches to show that the speaker receives the saving benefit.
Ahorrarme uses me for the speaker, and tiempo names what the speaker hopes to save.
The -iendo form presents joining as the means by which the time would be saved.
Me replaces se for the speaker and attaches to uniendo; the written accent preserves the original stress.
Directa takes its feminine singular form before -mente is added.

applications.exampleEs: UNIÉNDOME DIRECTAMENTE AL CLUB DE LA TAUTOLOGÍA
applications.explanationEn: Uniéndome supplies the speaker's joining action, while al is a plus el before the complete group name; directamente is an optional manner word inside the fragment.
Lo replaces the already mentioned club and stands before the changed verb voy.
Voy changes for the speaker, a links the two verbs, and crear stays in its unchanged -ar form for the planned action.
Cómo carries a written accent because it directly asks about the manner or source.
Supiste presents finding out as a completed past event.
Supiste already identifies one familiar listener, so the printed tú adds emphasis to who found out.
Supiste is the completed-past form of saber, and de introduces the people learned about; tú is an optional emphasized subject inside the fragment.

regions.labelEs: DE VUESTRO GRUPO DE FACEBOOK, “SI SE UNEN 1.000.000 DE PERSONAS A ESTE GRUPO, TENDRÁ 1.000.000 DE PERSONAS.”

excludedUnits.rationale: Facebook is the unchanged product and service name, not a Spanish lexical word in this line.
This printed numeral is excluded from the Spanish lexical inventory.
This second printed numeral is excluded from the Spanish lexical inventory; Vision omitted its initial 1 but bounded the complete visible number.

applications.explanationEn: Vuestro is the masculine singular possessive form for something belonging to several informally addressed people.

applications.exampleEs: SE UNEN 1.000.000 DE PERSONAS A ESTE GRUPO
applications.explanationEn: Se unen supplies the plural joining action, and a introduces the group being joined; the middle quantity supplies the subject.

applications.exampleEs: SI SE UNEN 1.000.000 DE PERSONAS A ESTE GRUPO, TENDRÁ 1.000.000 DE PERSONAS
applications.explanationEn: Si introduces the condition with present-form se unen, while tendrá states its future result; the numerals do not change that tense pattern.
Tendrá uses tener's irregular future stem tendr- plus the singular ending -á.

regions.labelEs: ¡ESCUCHAD! LA PRIMERA REGLA DEL CLUB DE LA TAUTOLOGÍA ES LA PRIMERA REGLA DEL CLUB DE LA TAUTOLOGÍA.

applications.explanationEn: Escuchad drops the final -r of escuchar and adds -d to command several informally addressed listeners.
The -ad command ending addresses several listeners informally as vosotros.
Primera appears before regla and uses feminine singular -a to match it.
The repeated ordinal again appears before regla with the matching feminine singular ending.

cards.questionEn: What does ¡Un momento! mean when someone interrupts or suddenly realizes something?
cards.answerEn: It means “Wait a moment!” or “Hold on!”
cards.noteEn: This fixed conversational interruption can ask someone to pause, or it can announce that the speaker has just noticed something important. Its function is broader than literally measuring one moment.

example.es: ¡Un momento! Creo que tengo la llave.
example.en: Hold on! I think I have the key.

cards.noteEn: Debo is the present form of deber used by the speaker. A following action stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: I must call Ana.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should or must do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of deber, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only deber changes for the person and time. Depending on context, deber can sound like advice, duty, or a strong requirement.

example.en: You should call Marta.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.

example.en: Do they have coffee?

cards.noteEn: Unirme is the dictionary-form verb unirse with me attached for the speaker. Unirse takes a before the group, organization, or activity being joined.

example.en: I want to join the team.

cards.questionEn: Where does me, te, se, nos, or os go when a verb used with one of those words stays in its dictionary form?
cards.answerEn: Attach the matching small word to the end: unir + me becomes unirme.
cards.noteEn: A pronominal verb is learned with se, such as unirse or acostarse. When its action verb remains in the unchanged dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, replace se with the form that matches the person and write it as part of the same word: acostarme, unirte, or irnos.

example.en: I want to go to bed early.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone joins a group or activity?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of unirse, then a, then name the group or activity.
cards.noteEn: The small part of unirse changes with the person: me uno, te unes, se une, nos unimos, os unís, or se unen. The word a remains before the group; a plus el contracts to al.

example.en: Lucía joined the team.

cards.answerEn: links unirse to the person or group being joined
cards.noteEn: Unirse (“to join”) takes a before the person, group, or activity being joined. English does not translate this a separately.

example.en: I want to join this group.

cards.questionEn: What is the usual Spanish expression for an honor society?
cards.noteEn: This is an association that recognizes members for academic achievement or another stated distinction. De honor identifies the type of society; honor stays singular.

example.es: La universidad tiene una sociedad de honor.
example.en: The university has an honor society.

cards.promptEs: sociedad de honor · club de la tautología
cards.questionEn: Why do the honor society and the Tautology Club form the joke?
cards.answerEn: The honor claim is circular, and the invented club repeatedly states facts that merely repeat themselves.
cards.noteEn: A tautology repeats the same idea or is true by definition. The club's membership promise says that a group with one million members will have one million members, while its first rule is simply identified as itself. The opening also mocks circular prestige: membership proves someone honorable because honorable people supposedly belong.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

example.en: I need a coffee cup.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.answerEn: to show or prove to someone
cards.noteEn: Demostrar means ‘to show’ or ‘to prove.’ The attached le marks the person receiving the proof; careful standard Spanish normally uses les when more than one receiver is meant.

example.es: Voy a demostrarle el resultado a Ana.
example.en: I am going to show Ana the result.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

example.en: I want to help you.

cards.questionEn: Why can Spanish use le or les with a verb and then still name the receiver with a phrase beginning with a?
cards.answerEn: Use le or les with the verb, then use a phrase beginning with the word a to identify the receiver explicitly.
cards.noteEn: Le is for one receiver and les for more than one. It normally appears before a conjugated verb, but it can attach to an unchanged verb form, as in darle. The later a phrase clarifies who or what the short marker refers to; Spanish often keeps both pieces even though natural English states the receiver only once. In the prompt, the slash means that le and les are alternatives, each plus sign means “followed by,” and the dots mean that other words may appear between the verb and the named receiver.

example.en: I gave the dog water.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Pertenezco is the present form of pertenecer used by the speaker. Pertenecer normally takes a before the group, category, or owner that something belongs to.

example.es: Pertenezco a un club de lectura.
example.en: I belong to a book club.

cards.promptEs: pertenecer a + grupo, categoría o persona
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something belongs to a group, category, or person?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of pertenecer, then a, then name what it belongs to.
cards.noteEn: Pertenecer changes for the person and time, while a stays before the group, category, or owner. Do not omit a even when English places ‘belong’ directly before another phrase in a different way.

example.es: Estos documentos pertenecen a la biblioteca.
example.en: These documents belong to the library.

cards.noteEn: Use pertenecer a before the group, category, or person that someone or something belongs to. English expresses this a as ‘to.’

example.en: This key belongs to Marta.

cards.noteEn: Básicamente summarizes something by its main or essential point.

example.es: Los dos planes son básicamente iguales.
example.en: The two plans are basically the same.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

example.en: Lucía answers clearly.

cards.answerEn: Parece que… means “It seems that…” or “It looks as though…”
cards.noteEn: Put a complete statement after que. Use this pattern when the available evidence points toward a conclusion, but you are not presenting that conclusion as completely certain.
cards.questionEn: How do you introduce something that seems likely but is not certain?

example.en: It looks like it is going to rain.

cards.noteEn: Podría is a form of poder used for a possible or imagined option. Here the unspoken subject is yo, so it means “I could.” The same written form can also go with one other person or thing when context supplies that subject.

example.en: I could call tomorrow.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

example.en: We can enter now.

cards.answerEn: to save myself; to spare myself (time or effort)
cards.noteEn: Ahorrarme joins me to ahorrar. With time, effort, or trouble after it, the form says that the speaker avoids spending or undergoing that amount.

example.es: Quiero ahorrarme una hora de espera.
example.en: I want to save myself an hour of waiting.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone saves themselves time?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of ahorrarse followed by tiempo or a specific amount of time.
cards.noteEn: The small word changes with the person: me ahorro, te ahorras, se ahorra, nos ahorramos, os ahorráis, or se ahorran. Tiempo names what is saved; other nouns such as esfuerzo or problemas can fill the same role.

example.es: Nos ahorramos tiempo con la lista.
example.en: We save time with the list.

cards.noteEn: Uniéndome is the -iendo action form of unirse with me attached for the speaker. The written accent keeps the original stress after me is added.

example.en: I learned a lot by joining the project.

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

example.en: She came in running.

cards.questionEn: How do you attach the matching marker of a pronominal verb to an ongoing-action form?
cards.answerEn: Join me, te, se, nos, os, or se to the end of the -ando or -iendo form, adding a written accent when needed to preserve the original stress.
cards.noteEn: A pronominal verb is learned with se, such as verse or prepararse. Its short marker changes with the person. When the marker follows an ongoing-action form as one word, spelling may need an accent: viendo + me becomes viéndome, and preparando + se becomes preparándose.

example.en: I am getting ready to leave.

cards.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

example.en: I’m going to the market.

cards.answerEn: tautology; a statement that needlessly repeats the same idea
cards.noteEn: A tautología says the same thing again in different words or is true simply because of how its terms are defined.

example.es: ‘Entrar dentro’ puede sonar como una tautología.
example.en: ‘Enter inside’ can sound like a tautology.

cards.noteEn: Ese points to a masculine singular noun that is not presented as right next to the speaker. Feminine singular is esa.

example.en: I do not recognize that sound.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

example.en: The movie—we watched it yesterday.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

example.en: I am going to study.

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)
Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

example.en: What is your name?

cards.answerEn: you found out; you learned (informal singular)
cards.noteEn: Supiste is the completed-past form of saber used with one familiar listener. In a question about a source, it asks how that person came to know something.

example.en: How did you find out the news?

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.questionEn: Why might Spanish say tú or yo when the verb already tells you who acts?
cards.answerEn: Say the subject pronoun to add emphasis, contrast, or clarity; otherwise Spanish often leaves it out.
cards.noteEn: A verb form such as eres already points to “you.” Adding tú can stress that particular person, especially in a contrast or a surprised question. The pronoun may appear after the verb.

example.en: I didn't go; you did.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone knows or has heard about a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of saber followed by de and the person or thing.
cards.noteEn: Saber changes for the person and time. De introduces the topic or person known about; depending on context, the expression can mean ‘know about,’ ‘hear about,’ or ‘have news of.’

example.en: Do you know about that project?

cards.answerEn: your (informal plural, before a masculine singular noun)

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what will happen if a real possibility occurs?
cards.answerEn: Use si with an ordinary present-time verb form for the condition, then state the result with a future form.
cards.noteEn: Si introduces a condition treated as genuinely possible. Spanish normally keeps the verb immediately after si in the present form, not the future. The result can use the future, built here by keeping the action verb and adding an ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.

example.en: If you finish early, we will have dinner together.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks unirse, ‘to join’
cards.noteEn: Unirse is used with me, te, se, nos, os, or se to match who joins. Se goes before the changed verb when the people joining are ‘they’ or formal ‘you all.’

example.en: They join the group.

cards.noteEn: Unen is the present form used with a plural third-person subject. With se and a, it means that those people join the following group or activity.

example.es: Muchas personas se unen al curso.
example.en: Many people join the course.

cards.answerEn: of; or no separate English word, linking an amount to what it measures
cards.noteEn: After a quantity expression, de introduces the substance or thing being measured. English uses “of” in expressions such as a lot of or the amount of, but may leave de untranslated in others, such as un poco de agua, “a little water.”

example.en: I want a little water.

cards.answerEn: it will have; he or she will have
cards.noteEn: Tendrá is a future form of tener for one person or thing. Tener changes its stem to tendr- before the future ending -á.

example.en: The building will have another entrance.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

example.en: Marta will call tomorrow.

cards.answerEn: listen (command to several people, mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Escuchad is the positive command form of escuchar for vosotros or vosotras. Most positive vosotros commands replace the dictionary form's final -r with -d: escuchar becomes escuchad.

example.en: Listen carefully, all of you.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para vosotros: hablad, comed, escribid
cards.questionEn: How do you tell several people informally to do something in Spain?
cards.answerEn: For most verbs, remove the final -r from the verb's dictionary form and add -d: hablar becomes hablad.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This positive command is used with vosotros or vosotras, mainly in Spain. If a short object word such as me is included, attach it to the end: ayudad + me becomes ayudadme.

example.en: Open your books.

cards.promptEs: número ordinal antes de un sustantivo
cards.questionEn: How do you use words such as first, second, or third before a Spanish noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the ordinal before the noun and make its ending match the noun's gender and number.
cards.noteEn: An ordinal gives a position in an order. Primero, segundo, tercero, último, and similar words usually come before the noun. Most forms use -o with a masculine singular noun and -a with a feminine singular noun, but primero and tercero shorten to primer and tercer before a masculine singular noun. Plural nouns use plural forms.

example.es: La segunda puerta está en el tercer piso.
example.en: The second door is on the third floor.

cards.noteEn: Del is the required contraction of de + el. It can mean “of the” or “from the,” depending on context.

example.en: I’m coming from the market.
